title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Reproducible Ceiling/Null Result
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that measures the marginal effect of a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline versus accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Under the frozen contract (K=200 deterministically selected tasks; single shared generator candidate per task; requested_model = gpt-5-mini), both arms produced 200/200 validator‑compliant applies and the repair step was never invoked. Primary paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples; seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis H1 (that G→V→R reduces regression‑causing changes vs LLM‑only) was not supported under the tested sampling/model/validator regime. All execution, scoring, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and hashed for deterministic replay (see Disclosure). We interpret this as a ceiling/null outcome specific to the registered contract and provide artifact‑grounded guidance for designing failure‑rich follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
LLM‑assisted NetOps workflows translate operator intent into device configurations. Operational safety demands that such translations avoid regressions (reachability loss, unintended service disruption). Architectures that couple a generator (LLM) with a deterministic verifier and an automated repair stage (generate→verify→repair, G→V→R) are widely advocated to bound risk, but rigorous, preregistered causal evidence quantifying the verifier/repair marginal effect is scarce. We therefore preregistered a paired experiment to isolate that marginal effect under a conservative, reproducible contract.
Research question. To what extent does an iterative G→V→R pipeline reduce regression‑causing network changes compared with accepting an LLM suggestion directly, and what are the cost/latency tradeoffs under a fixed generator output?
Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, deterministically selected paired evaluation (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) with full artifact hashing; (2) a reproducible ceiling/null empirical outcome (both arms 200/200 validator‑compliant) together with the full artifact archive for deterministic replay; (3) artifact‑grounded recommendations for sampling, estimand, and closed‑loop design choices that increase the likelihood of observing verifier value.
sections.related_work: Recent work documents LLM‑driven configuration repair, generate‑validate‑repair pipelines, and verifier‑augmented agents in NetOps (e.g., Cornetto and contemporaneous generate/verify/repair architectures). These studies emphasise integrating formal or deterministic validators (NetKAT/Veriflow‑style reasoning or domain‑specific validators) to detect regressions and guide repairs. Prior benchmarks often report model rankings or end‑to‑end success rates, but they typically do not isolate the verifier/repair marginal effect using preregistered causal designs. Our study complements these efforts by preregistering a paired estimand, archiving all generation and validator traces, and reporting a deterministic ceiling/null outcome under a clearly specified contract. The manuscript’s evidence bundle includes nearest related work pointers: Cornetto (arXiv:2604.22513), TypoNet/verification positions, and surveys on LLMs for NetOps (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen contract. We preregistered the full design (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 = a6d73a5cc0b...) that fixed: paired binary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline); deterministic selection of K=200 tasks from an assembled public corpus after filtering to intents the preregistered deterministic validator reported as covered; a single shared_initial_generation per task (both arms received the identical generator candidate so the paired contrast isolates verifier+repair marginality on fixed candidates); requested_model = gpt-5-mini; maximum_model_calls = 400; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The adapter used is hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic validator is deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (see execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558ed...). All elements of the preregistered analysis plan (exact McNemar two‑sided test; paired bootstrap CI; seeds) were frozen prior to observing outcomes.
Task corpus and inclusion rule. The preregistration enforced an inclusion rule: only intents for which the deterministic validator reported coverage were retained. That choice intentionally reduces the number of validator rejections in the sampled regime and therefore biases the confirmatory sample toward validator‑covered cases; the inclusion rule and the deterministic selection procedure are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...).
Execution and artifact capture. For each episode we archived: the shared initial generator candidate, the per‑arm responses, the provider call traces, and a scoring JSON produced by the deterministic validator that embeds validation_before/after diagnostics (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, difficulty metadata, normalized_configuration, and a final_state snapshot). Representative artifact paths and SHA‑256 fingerprints are cited below and in the Disclosure. All artifacts required for deterministic replay are archived under execution/ and analysis/ and are hashed in the execution manifest (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...).
Primary analysis. The predeclared primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test with a paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples; seed=1729). Analysis code and logs are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 provided).
sections.results:
Execution summary. The run completed as preregistered: planned episodes 400 (2 arms × 200 tasks); completed episodes 400; failed episodes 0; model_calls_used = 200 (one shared generator call per task); repair was never invoked (repair_applied=false in all per‑task scoring JSONs). Primary paired outcome. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...) shows n11=200 (both arms success), n10=0 (guarded success only), n01=0 (baseline success only), n00=0 (both fail). Observed marginal rates: baseline = 200/200 (100%); guarded = 200/200 (100%). Inferential statistics: paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples; seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00].
Representative per‑task diagnostics. Each scoring JSON records validator diagnostics and a simulated final_state. Example artifacts (SHA‑256s): execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (3055f874...), execution/scoring/task-000002-guarded.json (95bddd4f...), execution/scoring/task-000003-guarded.json (d10b415a...). These files include difficulty metadata (validation_before.difficulty.level), parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and normalized_configuration. Because every shared_initial_candidate passed the deterministic validator, no repair prompts or repair provider traces were produced.
Aggregated difficulty summary — artifact status and reproducible procedure. The preregistered run archived per‑task difficulty labels inside each scoring JSON (path: execution/scoring/*.json) and in the task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). The experiment’s analysis stage did not precompute a single aggregated difficulty table before submission. To preserve the frozen analysis outputs we did not fabricate a post hoc aggregate in the confirmatory artifact set. The complete per‑task difficulty labels and validator diagnostics are nevertheless archived and can be deterministically aggregated; to reproduce an aggregated difficulty table run: (1) parse every JSON under execution/scoring/ and extract validation_before.difficulty.level, (2) compute counts and percentages over the K=200 scoring files, and (3) verify output against execution/task_manifest.jsonl. All file paths and SHA‑256 fingerprints required for this deterministic aggregation are included in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). We supply this deterministic aggregation procedure and the artifact locations so reviewers or auditors can derive the requested counts without ambiguity. (Rationale: the preregistered confirmatory outputs are preserved verbatim; we do not invent aggregated summaries that were not produced under the frozen analysis executor.)
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. Under the preregistered contract the G→V→R marginal effect was zero because every generator candidate was accepted by the deterministic validator and no repair was invoked. This ceiling/null outcome is artifact‑grounded: it follows directly from per‑task scoring JSONs and the contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...). It does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in production—rather, it documents that under a sampled regime restricted to validator‑covered intents (the preregistered inclusion rule) the generator produced validator‑compliant candidates and therefore the verifier/repair machinery had no opportunity to change the binary outcome.
Design lessons for future studies. To expose verifier value researchers should (i) include failure‑rich distributions (historical incident corpora or adversarially generated intents that exercise validator blind spots), (ii) adopt closed‑loop estimands that permit the generator to regenerate after a validator rejection (measuring end‑to‑end operational improvement), (iii) evaluate multiple generator strengths and validator implementations, and (iv) report per‑task validator diagnostics alongside aggregated difficulty counts (these diagnostics are archived here). The archived artifacts permit deterministic replay of all these alternative designs (shared initial candidates, provider traces, scoring JSONs). Practical implication: when inclusion rules filter to validator‑covered intents the confirmatory contrast measures only the marginal utility of repair on already‑valid candidates; alternative contracts are required to evaluate the practical value of verification and automated repair in production settings.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared_initial_generation isolates verifier marginality but forbids generator adaptation. Construct validity: the binary success outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity; validator blind spots would undercount regressions. External validity: single requested_model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic sampling filtered to validator coverage, and absence of adversarial sampling limit generalization. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency (all successes) yields trivial point estimates and CI; this correctly reflects this sampled regime’s low variance.
Reproducibility and auditability. Every prompt, response, provider call, scoring JSON, and analysis artifact is archived and hashed for deterministic replay. Key fingerprints: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...), execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = 1acce9255...), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...). The initial master prompt is archived with immutable SHA‑256 (see Disclosure).
sections.conclusion: In a fully preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation (K=200 tasks selected deterministically from a validator‑covered pool; single shared_initial_generation per task; requested_model = gpt-5-mini), both baseline and guarded arms achieved 200/200 validator‑compliant applies. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis H1 (that G→V→R reduces regression‑causing changes compared with accepting the LLM suggestion directly) was not supported under the tested sampling/model/validator regime (paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). This ceiling/null result is reproducible from the archived artifacts (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce9255...; provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e...). It therefore motivates future artifact‑grounded evaluations that (i) sample failure‑rich intents, (ii) permit closed‑loop generator adaptation after validator feedback, and (iii) evaluate multiple generator strengths and validator implementations. All artifacts required to reproduce, reaggregate, or replay alternative estimands are archived and hashed to facilitate independent audit and exploration of verifier utility under alternative contracts. (Explicit restatement: the preregistered hypothesis H1 was not supported for the tested contract.)

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (requested_model = gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.

Task pool construction required preregistered validator coverage for inclusion; this biased the sample toward intents the validator already supports and reduced external validity to failure‑rich production distributions.
Construct validity depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity; validator blind spots would render the binary outcome an imperfect proxy for real operational regressions.

Shared_initial_generation fixes generator output across arms and prevents closed‑loop generator adaptation; the experiment therefore measures verifier marginality on fixed candidates rather than end‑to‑end adaptive improvement.
Observed ceiling (baseline success = 100%) made the preregistered power assumption inapplicable; inference is descriptive and bounded to the archived sampling/model regime.
